content: A refreshable Braille display, also known as a Braille terminal, is an electro-mechanical device designed to present Braille characters. It achieves this by raising dots through holes on a flat surface. This device is primarily used by blind computer users who are unable to rely on a standard computer monitor to read text output. In addition to refreshable Braille displays, speech synthesizers are also commonly employed for the same purpose. Depending on the situation, a blind user may alternate between these two systems or use them simultaneously. Due to the intricate engineering required to create a durable and reliable display capable of withstanding daily wear and tear, refreshable Braille displays are expensive. Typically, these devices display 40 or 80 Braille cells, although some models, particularly those integrated into notetaker devices, may feature 18 to 40 cells. Certain models indicate the cursor's position by vibrating the dots, while others include a switch for each cell, allowing the user to move the cursor directly to a specific cell. The mechanism that raises the Braille dots operates using the piezoelectric effect. This involves specific crystals that expand when a voltage is applied to them. These crystals are connected to levers, which in turn raise the dots to form Braille characters. Each character is represented by a combination of up to eight dots. The software responsible for controlling the display is referred to as a screen reader. This software extracts the content displayed on the screen from the operating system, converts it into Braille characters, and transmits it to the Braille display. Screen readers designed for graphical operating systems are particularly complex, as they must interpret and describe graphical elements such as windows and sliders in text form. Modern operating systems often include an Application Programming Interface (API) to assist screen readers in accessing this information, such as Microsoft Active Accessibility (MSAA) for Windows or Assistive Technology Service Provider Interface (AT-SPI) for GNOME. In 2000, a new innovation called the rotating-wheel Braille display was developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Another rotating display was later designed by Leuven University in Belgium. However, both designs are still in the process of commercialization. In this system, Braille dots are placed on the edge of a spinning wheel, allowing the user to read continuously with a stationary finger while the wheel rotates at a chosen speed. The Braille dots are set in a scanning-style manner as the wheel spins past a stationary actuator that configures the Braille characters. This design significantly reduces manufacturing complexity, making rotating-wheel Braille displays much more affordable than traditional refreshable Braille displays. The foundation of a refreshable Braille display lies in the concept of a pure Braille terminal. In such devices, input is typically performed using two sets of three keys along with a space bar, similar to the Perkins Brailler. Output is provided via a refreshable Braille display consisting of a row of electromechanical character cells, each capable of raising or lowering a combination of six round-tipped pins. Variants of these devices exist, including those that use a conventional QWERTY keyboard for input and Braille pins for output, as well as devices designed solely for input or output. In 1951, David Abraham, a woodworking teacher at Perkins, developed a portable Braille terminal, marking a significant milestone in the history of Braille technology.
